facts.statement: The genus Rubeosaurus was proposed as a synonym for Styracosaurus by McDonald and Horner in 2010.
facts.quote: synonyms: *RubeosaurusMcDonald & Horner, 2010

facts.statement: Styracosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913

facts.statement: Styracosaurus fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian)

facts.statement: Styracosaurus reached lengths of 5 to 5.5 meters and weighed between 1.8 and 2.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus was a relatively large dinosaur, reaching lengths of 5 - 5.5 m and weighing about 1.8 - 2.7 MT.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus stood approximately 1.8 meters tall.
facts.quote: It stood about 1.8 m tall.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a relatively short tail.
facts.quote: Its tail was rather short.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a beak and shearing cheek teeth in continuous dental batteries, indicating a diet of sliced plants.
facts.quote: The skull had a beak and shearing cheek teeth arranged in continuous dental batteries, suggesting that the animal sliced up plants.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus likely lived in large herds, a behavior suggested by bone bed discoveries.
facts.quote: Like other ceratopsians, this dinosaur may have been a herd animal, travelling in large groups, as suggested by bone beds.

facts.statement: The first Styracosaurus fossil was discovered in the summer of 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg.
facts.quote: The first fossil of Styracosaurus was discovered in the summer of 1913 by American palaeontologist Charles H. Sternberg

facts.statement: The first skull was found on the southwest bank of the Red Deer River, about 12 miles below the mouth of Berry Creek, in the Belly River Formation.
facts.quote: Sternberg discovered the skull on the southwest bank of the Red Deer River about 12 mi below the mouth of Berry Creek in what was then called the Belly River Formation.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe described the first skull as the holotype of Styracosaurus albertensis in 1913.
facts.quote: This mostly complete skull was described in 1913 by Canadian palaeontologist Lawrence Lambe as the holotype of the new ceratopsian Styracosaurus albertensis.

facts.statement: Levi Sternberg excavated the mandible and skeleton of the type individual in 1935 for the Royal Ontario Museum.
facts.quote: In 1935, the quarry was revisited by Levi Sternberg, son of Charles H., in part of a field crew of the Royal Ontario Museum, where the mandible and largely complete skeleton of the same individual were excavated.

facts.statement: The original quarry is now located within Dinosaur Provincial Park in the Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: The quarry and sediments are now within the boundaries of Dinosaur Provincial Park and the Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: The Canadian Museum of Nature acquired the reunited type skeleton in 1955, cataloging it as CMN 344.
facts.quote: Negotiations concluded in 1955 allowing the Canadian Museum of Nature to acquire this mandible and skeleton, reuniting the full type individual of Styracosaurus, now under the accession number CMN 344.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown collected a Styracosaurus specimen in 1915 from the middle fork of Sand Creek, 12 miles downstream of Steveville.
facts.quote: American palaeontologist Barnum Brown collected another specimen of Styracosaurus in 1915 from the same horizon as the type, but from the middle fork of Sand Creek 12 mi downstream of Steveville.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown and Erich Maren Schlaikjer named the species S. parksi in 1937 based on a specimen collected by Brown.
facts.quote: Brown and American palaeontologist Erich Maren Schlaikjer reidentified it as a nearly complete skeleton and partial skull of a new species of Styracosaurus, which they described and named S. parksi in 1937.

facts.statement: The locality of the S. parksi specimen was relocated in 2006 by Darren Tanke in the upper Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: in 2006 it was relocated by Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology in the upper portion of the Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: A nearly complete skull and skeleton were found in 1989 at Sage Creek, about 130 km southeast of the holotype.
facts.quote: A nearly complete skull and skeleton (TMP 1989.97.1) was found in 1989 at Sage Creek only 10 m below the prairie level in the coulee, but approximately 130 km southeast of the holotype

facts.statement: A nearly complete skull and partial skeleton were discovered in August 2008 and collected in August 2009 by the Royal Tyrrell Museum crew in Princess Coulee.
facts.quote: Another nearly complete skull and partial skeleton (TMP 2009.80.1) was discovered in August 2008 and collected in August 2009 by the crew of the Royal Tyrrell Museum in the central fork of Princess Coulee just south of Dinosaur Provincial Park.

facts.statement: A large Styracosaurus skeleton was found in May 2015 along Matzhiwin Creek near Duchess, Alberta, by the University of Alberta.
facts.quote: In May 2015 a skeleton of a large Styracosaurus was found along Matzhiwin Creek near the town of Duchess, Alberta around 18 km west of Dinosaur Provincial Park by the University of Alberta

facts.statement: The skull of the Duchess specimen was described in 2020, while the skeleton remains under preparation.
facts.quote: The skull of the specimen (UALVP 55900) was described in 2020 but the skeleton remains under preparation

facts.statement: The function of Styracosaurus horns and frills has been debated for many years.
facts.quote: The function or functions of the horns and frills have been debated for many years.

facts.statement: The classification of S. ovatus is debated, having been moved to Rubeosaurus in 2010 but potentially returned to Styracosaurus or considered a separate genus again since 2020.
facts.quote: Another species, S. ovatus, named in 1930 by Charles Gilmore was reassigned to a new genus, Rubeosaurus, by Andrew McDonald and Jack Horner in 2010, but it has been considered either its own genus or a species of Styracosaurus (or even a specimen of S. albertensis) again, since 2020.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus albertensis was approximately 5.5 to 5.8 meters long and stood about 1.65 meters high at the hips.
facts.quote: These fossils indicate that S. albertensis was around 5.5-5.8 m in length and stood about 1.65 m high at the hips.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown and his team collected a nearly complete articulated skeleton of Styracosaurus in 1915 while working for the American Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown and crew, working for the American Museum of Natural History in New York, collected a nearly complete articulated skeleton with a partial skull in 1915.

facts.statement: Fossils of Styracosaurus were found in the Dinosaur Park Formation near Steveville, Alberta.
facts.quote: These fossils were also found in the Dinosaur Park Formation, near Steveville, Alberta.

facts.statement: Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum relocated the site of the S. parksi fossils in the summer of 2006.
facts.quote: In the summer of 2006, Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology in Drumheller, Alberta relocated the long lost S. parksi site.

facts.statement: The species Styracosaurus parksi is now accepted as a specimen of Styracosaurus albertensis.
facts.quote: It is now accepted as a specimen of S. albertensis.

facts.statement: Several species previously assigned to Styracosaurus have been reassigned to other genera.
facts.quote: Several other species which were assigned to Styracosaurus have since been assigned to other genera.

facts.statement: S. sphenocerus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius and later attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.
facts.quote: S. sphenocerus, described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius and based on a nasal bone with a broken Styracosaurus-like straight nose horn, was attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus ovatus was described by Gilmore in 1930 based on a partial parietal bone from the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: A species, Styracosaurus ovatus, from the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, was described by Gilmore in 1930, named for a partial parietal under the accession number USNM 11869.

facts.statement: Unlike S. albertensis, the longest parietal spikes of S. ovatus converge towards their tips rather than projecting parallel behind the frill.
facts.quote: Unlike S. albertensis, the longest parietal spikes converge towards their tips, instead of projecting parallel behind the frill.

facts.statement: The parietal spikes of S. ovatus are much shorter than those of S. albertensis, with the longest measuring only 295 mm.
facts.quote: As estimated from the preserved material, the spikes are much shorter than in S. albertensis, with the longest only 295 mm long.

facts.statement: McDonald and Horner reclassified S. ovatus into the new genus Rubeosaurus.
facts.quote: McDonald and Horner gave the species the new genus name Rubeosaurus.

facts.statement: Robert Holmes and colleagues considered S. ovatus to be a junior synonym of S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Holmes et al. considering the latter a junior synonym of the former.

facts.statement: John Wilson and colleagues advised retaining S. ovatus as a separate species of Styracosaurus, possibly directly descended from S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Wilson and colleagues advised that S. ovatus was retained as a separate, probably directly descended from S. albertensis, species of Styracosaurus.

facts.statement: Adult Styracosaurus measured approximately 5 to 5.5 meters in length and weighed between 1.8 and 2.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Individuals of the genus Styracosaurus were approximately 5 - 5.5 m long as adults and weighed about 1.8 - 2.7 MT.

facts.statement: The skull of Styracosaurus featured a large nostril, a tall straight nasal horn, and a neck frill topped with at least four large spikes.
facts.quote: The skull was massive, with a large nostril, a tall straight nose horn, and a parietal squamosal frill (a neck frill) crowned with at least four large spikes.

facts.statement: The four longest spikes on the neck frill of Styracosaurus were 50 to 55 centimeters long, similar in length to the nasal horn.
facts.quote: Each of the four longest frill spines was comparable in length to the nose horn, at 50 to 55 cm long.

facts.statement: Lambe estimated the nasal horn of the type specimen to be 57 centimeters long, though the tip was not preserved.
facts.quote: The nasal horn was estimated by Lambe at 57 cm long in the type specimen, but the tip had not been preserved.

facts.statement: Subadult Styracosaurus possessed modest pyramid-shaped brow horns that were replaced by pits in adults.
facts.quote: Modest pyramid-shaped brow horns were present in subadults, but were replaced by pits in adults.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a toothless beak at the front of its mouth.
facts.quote: The front of the mouth had a toothless beak.

facts.statement: Each toe of Styracosaurus ended in a hoof-like claw sheathed in horn.
facts.quote: Each toe bore a hooflike ungual which was sheathed in horn.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests that Styracosaurus likely held its legs in an intermediate crouched position rather than sprawled or directly underneath its body.
facts.quote: The most recent work has put forward an intermediate crouched position as most likely.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is classified as a member of the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus is a member of the Centrosaurinae.

facts.statement: There is significant debate regarding the validity of certain centrosaurine genera, including whether Centrosaurus and Monoclonius are distinct genera, undiagnosable, or represent sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: Because of the variation between species and even individual specimens of centrosaurines, there has been much debate over which genera and species are valid, particularly whether Centrosaurus and/or Monoclonius are valid genera, undiagnosable, or possibly members of the opposite sex.

facts.statement: In 1996, Peter Dodson argued that sufficient variation existed to classify Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus, and Monoclonius as separate genera, noting Styracosaurus was more similar to Centrosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1996, Peter Dodson found enough variation between Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus, and Monoclonius to warrant separate genera, and that Styracosaurus resembled Centrosaurus more closely than either resembled Monoclonius.

facts.statement: Most researchers do not accept Monoclonius nasicornis as a female Styracosaurus but consider it a synonym of Centrosaurus apertus.
facts.quote: However, most other researchers have not accepted Monoclonius nasicornis as a female Styracosaurus, instead regarding it as a synonym of Centrosaurus apertus.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that Styracosaurus albertensis evolved directly from Centrosaurus and subsequently into the later species Rubeosaurus ovatus.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that Styracosaurus albertensis is a direct descendant of Centrosaurus (C. apertus or C. nasicornis), and that it in turn evolved directly into the slightly later species Rubeosaurus ovatus.

facts.statement: A bone bed containing Styracosaurus remains is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
facts.quote: A bone bed composed of Styracosaurus remains is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, about halfway up the formation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the mass death of Styracosaurus at the Dinosaur Park Formation site may have resulted from non-herding animals gathering at a waterhole during a drought in a seasonal, semi-arid environment.
facts.quote: The mass deaths at this site may have been a result of otherwise non-herding animals congregating around a waterhole in a period of drought, with evidence suggesting the environment may have been seasonal and semi-arid.

facts.statement: Paleontologists Gregory Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that Styracosaurus could run faster than an elephant based on trackway evidence lacking sprawling forelimb signs.
facts.quote: Paleontologists Gregory Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that large ceratopsians such as Styracosaurus were able to run faster than an elephant, based on possible ceratopsian trackways which did not exhibit signs of sprawling forelimbs.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus were herbivores that likely fed mostly on low-growing vegetation due to the position of their heads.
facts.quote: Styracosaurs were herbivorous dinosaurs; they probably fed mostly on low growth because of the position of the head.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus may have been capable of knocking down taller plants using their horns, beak, and body mass.
facts.quote: They may, however, have been able to knock down taller plants with their horns, beak, and bulk.

facts.statement: Unlike hadrosaurids, the teeth of Styracosaurus were adapted for slicing rather than grinding.
facts.quote: Unlike hadrosaurids, which also had dental batteries, ceratopsid teeth sliced but did not grind.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the specific diet of Styracosaurus, with some scientists suggesting they ate palms and cycads while others propose ferns.
facts.quote: Some scientists have suggested that ceratopsids like Styracosaurus ate palms and cycads, while others have suggested ferns.

facts.statement: Peter Dodson has proposed that Late Cretaceous ceratopsians like Styracosaurus may have knocked down angiosperm trees to shear off leaves and twigs.
facts.quote: Dodson has proposed that Late Cretaceous ceratopsians may have knocked down angiosperm trees and then sheared off leaves and twigs.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus possessed large nasal horns and frills that were among the most distinctive facial features of all dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The large nasal horns and frills of Styracosaurus are among the most distinctive facial adornments of all dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The function of Styracosaurus horns and frills has been debated since the discovery of the first horned dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Their function has been the subject of debate since the first horned dinosaurs were discovered.

facts.statement: A skull discovered in 2015 suggested that individual variation was likely common within the Styracosaurus genus.
facts.quote: A skull discovered in 2015 from a Styracosaurus indicates that individual variation was likely commonplace in the genus.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus fossils are known from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation

facts.statement: The Dinosaur Park Formation environment was a low-relief area of rivers and floodplains that became swampier and influenced by marine conditions as the Western Interior Seaway expanded.
facts.quote: The Dinosaur Park Formation is interpreted as a low-relief setting of rivers and floodplains that became more swampy and influenced by marine conditions over time as the Western Interior Seaway transgressed westward.

facts.statement: The climate where Styracosaurus lived was warmer than modern Alberta, without frost, but featured wetter and drier seasons.
facts.quote: The climate was warmer than present-day Alberta, without frost, but with wetter and drier seasons.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus ovatus lived alongside diverse fauna including ornithopods, hadrosaurids, other centrosaurines, leptoceratopsids, ankylosaurs, the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus, and smaller theropods in the Two Medicine Formation.
facts.quote: In the Two Medicine Formation, dinosaurs that lived alongside Styracosaurus ovatus included the basal ornithopod Orodromeus, hadrosaurids (such as Hypacrosaurus, Maiasaura, and Prosaurolophus), the centrosaurines Brachyceratops and Einiosaurus, the leptoceratopsid Cerasinops, the ankylosaurs Edmontonia and Euoplocephalus, the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus (which appears to have been a specialist of preying on ceratopsians), as well as the smaller theropods Bambiraptor, Chirostenotes, Troodon, and Avisaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Styracosaurus was named by Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Lambe, 1913

facts.statement: The species Styracosaurus albertensis was named by Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: species_authority: Lambe, 1913

facts.statement: Styracosaurus has had several synonyms including Centrosaurus nasicornis, Monoclonius nasicornis, Styracosaurus parksi, Styracosaurus ovatus, and Rubeosaurus ovatus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Centrosaurus nasicornis Brown, 1917 Centrosaurus nasicornus Brown, 1917 Monoclonius nasicornis Brown, 1917 Monoclonius nasicornus Brown, 1917 Styracosaurus parksi Brown & Schlaikjer, 1937 Styracosaurus ovatus Gilmore, 1930? Rubeosaurus ovatus McDonald & Horner, 2010?

facts.statement: Styracosaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: Vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus was relatively large, measuring 5.5 meters in length, 1.8 meters in height, and weighing 2.4 tons.
facts.quote: Eran relativamente grandes, tenían 5,5 metros de longitud, 1,8 de altura y pesaban 2,4 toneladas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had robust legs, a bulky body, and a short tail.
facts.quote: Poseía patas robustas, un cuerpo voluminoso y cola corta.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a beak and cutting molars arranged in continuous dental batteries, suggesting it cut plants.
facts.quote: Tenía un pico y muelas cortantes dispuestas en baterías dentales continuas, lo que sugiere que el animal cortaba plantas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus's most notable feature was a cranial shield with four to six long parietal spikes extending from the neck, two jugal horns under its eyes, and one horn over its snout.
facts.quote: Su característica más notable es un escudo cefálico provisto de cuatro a seis púas parietales largas que se extendían desde el cuello, dos cuernos yugales bajo sus ojos y otro sobre su hocico.

facts.statement: The cranial shield of Styracosaurus could reach 60 centimeters in length and 15 centimeters in width.
facts.quote: Este llegaba alcanzar 60 centímetros de largo y 15 de ancho.

facts.statement: The discovery of 100 individuals at an Arizona site suggests that Styracosaurus lived in herds like other ceratopsians.
facts.quote: En el yacimiento de Arizona se descubrieron 100 individuos, lo que indica que, como otros ceratópsidos, vivían en manadas.

facts.statement: Adult Styracosaurus measured approximately 5.5 meters in length and weighed about 2.7 tons.
facts.quote: Los individuos adultos del género Styracosaurus midieron aproximadamente 5,5 metros de largo cuando y pesaban de las 2,7 toneladas.

facts.statement: The skull was large and massive, featuring a large snout, a large high nasal horn, and a frill topped with at least four long spikes.
facts.quote: El cráneo era grande y masivo, con un gran morro, con un cuerno en el hocico grande y alto, y una excrecencia parietoescamosa, la gola nucal, coronada con al menos 4 largas espinas.

facts.statement: The neck spikes were comparable in length to the nasal horn, measuring between 50 and 55 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Cada una de estas espinas del cuello es comparable con las del hocico, de entre 50 a 55 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: The nasal horn is estimated to be 57 centimeters long in the holotype specimen, though it is only partially complete.
facts.quote: El cuerno nasal se estima en 57 centímetros en el espécimen holotipico, pero este cuerno solo esta parcialmente completo.

facts.statement: Small pyramid-shaped brow horns were present in subadults but were replaced by pits in adults.
facts.quote: Modestos cuernos en las cejas en forma de pirámide estaban presentes en los subadultos, pero fueron reemplazados por fosas en los adultos.

facts.statement: The front of the mouth had a toothless beak.
facts.quote: El frente de la boca tenía un pico desdentado.

facts.statement: The robust body of Styracosaurus resembles that of rhinoceroses.
facts.quote: El robusto cuerpo de Styracosaurus recuerda a los de los rinocerontes.

facts.statement: Each toe had a shape and structure similar to the hooves of modern ungulates, covered in keratin.
facts.quote: Cada dedo del pie tenía una forma y estructura similar al de los cascos de los ungulados modernos, forrado en queratina.

facts.statement: Recent work has proposed an intermediate crouched posture as the most likely stance for Styracosaurus.
facts.quote: El trabajo más reciente ha propuesto una posición agachada intermedia como muy probable.

facts.statement: Paleontologists Gregory S. Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that large ceratopsians like Styracosaurus could walk faster than an elephant, based on trackways showing no signs of front limb extension.
facts.quote: Los paleontólogos Gregory S. Paul y Per Christiansen del Museo Zoológico de la Universidad de Copenhague en Dinamarca propusieron que los ceratopsianos grandes tales como Styracosaurus podían caminar más rápidamente que un elefante, basado en las posibles huellas de un ceratopsianos, el cual no exhibe muestras signos de esxteción de los miembros delanteros.

facts.statement: The first fossil remains of Styracosaurus were collected in Alberta, Canada, by C.M. Sternberg from the Dinosaur Park Formation and named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos fósiles de Styracosaurus fueron recogidos de Alberta, Canadá por C.M. Sternberg, del área hoy conocida como Parque Provincial del Dinosaurio, en la formación geológica actualmente conocida como Formación Dinosaur Park y nombrado por Lawrence Lambe en 1913.

facts.statement: The generic name is formed from the Greek words styrax, meaning 'spike' or 'thorn', and sauros, meaning 'lizard'.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico está formado por las palabras griegas στύραξ, styrax, —espina, púa— y σαῦρος, sauros, —lagarto—.

facts.statement: The specific epithet refers to the Latinized toponym of the Canadian province where the fossils were found, Alberta.
facts.quote: El epíteto específico hace referencia al topónimo latinizado del estado canadiense donde se hallaron sus restos fósiles, Alberta.

facts.statement: In the summer of 2006, Darren Tanke of the Tyrrell Museum in Drumheller, Alberta, rediscovered the original lost site of S. parksi.
facts.quote: En el verano de 2006, Darren Tanke del Museo Tyrrell en Drumheller, Alberta reencontraron el sitio original perdido de S. parksi.

facts.statement: Pieces of the skull, evidently abandoned by the 1915 team, were found at the site.
facts.quote: Pedazos del cráneo, abandonados evidentemente por el equipo 1915, fueron encontrados en el yacimiento.

facts.statement: At least one confirmed site, site 42, exists in the Dinosaur Provincial Park.
facts.quote: Al menos existe un yacimiento confirmado, yacimiento 42, en el Parque Provincial de los Dinosaurios

facts.statement: Styracosaurus belongs to the parent group Centrosaurini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Centrosaurini

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is classified in the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Family: Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Styracosaurus belongs to the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Styracosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is hoped that more pieces will be found, perhaps enough to authorize a redescription of the skull and to test if S. albertensis and S. parksi are synonyms.
facts.quote: Se espera que más pedazos seán encontrados, quizá los suficientes para autorizar una redescripción del cráneo y la prueba si S. albertensis y S. parksi son sinónimos.
